text.en: Khushi reaches school early, and the sunlight makes the classroom bright and beautiful. She draws what she sees and asks herself where all these things come from, who made them and what they are made of. We help her find out about materials such as wood, metal and glass, and learn to group things as solid, liquid or gas, and as natural or artificial.

The table, chair and door are made of wood, which comes from trees. The hinges, nails and latches of the door are made of metal. Metals are taken from rocks called ore that are dug out from inside the Earth. Common metals are iron, copper, aluminium, gold and silver. Mercury, the metal in a thermometer, is a liquid. An alloy is a mixture of metals. Steel, brass and bronze are alloys. Windowpanes and bulbs are made of glass, which is mostly made of sand. Electric switches are made of plastic. A material is the stuff that a thing is made of. Different things can be made of the same material, and one thing can have more than one material.
Khushi could see a tree through the glass window pane, without noticing the glass. Things that we can see through clearly are transparent, and most glass is transparent. Things that we cannot see through at all are opaque. Wood is opaque. Things that let some light through but not a clear picture are translucent. A lamp shade made of paper is translucent. Looking at a white paper through thin coloured plastic or glass can make it look the colour of that plastic. We should never look at the sun directly, because it harms our eyes.
Different materials feel and sound different. Metal feels cold and shiny, and it makes a ting sound when we tap it. Wood sounds like thak. A table cannot be made of fabric because fabric is soft and flexible, and a table has to be hard and rigid. Fabric is good for clothes and curtains because it bends. Some pairs are odd, such as an umbrella made of paper. Paper tears in the rain. Materials are chosen for what they can do. Their properties, such as hard, soft, bendy, shiny, rough and smooth, tell us how to use them.
Things that do not change their shape are solids, like a stone, a spoon, a bottle, a bag and ice. Water does not keep its shape. It flows and takes the shape of the cup, so it is a liquid. Ink and honey are also liquids. Air does not stay in a cup. It floats in and out and spreads everywhere. Air is a gas, and so are smoke and steam. Some things are confusing, such as sand, a sponge or clay. We have to look at how they behave.
Things that exist naturally in nature are called natural, such as a mango tree, a mango, a bird, rocks, water and air. Natural things may be alive or not alive. Things made by people are artificial, such as clothes, shoes and tables. Khushi drew a mango tree with a mango on it, so she might have drawn it around June, the time when mangoes ripen. Plastic, petrol and rubber can be made artificially from petroleum, a liquid found deep underground.
Khushi reached school early, and sunlight shone through the windows so brightly that she wanted to draw the scene. Can you name everything Khushi drew? Draw your own classroom in your notebook and label the things in it. Khushi wondered where all these things came from, who made them and what they were made of, so let us help her find out.
Find as many things or parts of things made of metal as you can, such as hinges, nails, latches and utensils. If you do not know the name of a metal, ask a friend or an elder, and make a list of the metals you recognise in your notebook. Think about what mats, bulbs and electric switches are made of, because not everything in the classroom is wood or metal.
Khushi was sitting at her desk and could see a tree full of flowers, and when she reached out she touched a glass pane she had not even noticed. Collect small objects of different materials, such as bottles, papers, cloth and utensils, and look at a light bulb or a candle flame through them. You can see through some objects very clearly, through some only partly, and through some not at all, so arrange them in that order. Take care: never look at the sun continuously, through any object or directly, because it will harm your eyes. Name one more material that is transparent, and find some materials that are translucent.
Collect two or three see-through bags, bottles or thin cloths of different colours and look at a sheet of white paper through them. Does the white paper look different through thin blue or thin yellow plastic or glass? How does a blue object look through thin yellow plastic? Try to recall times when you looked through coloured transparent things before.
In the chain game, Khushi groups objects by material: wood for the table, chair and door; metal for hinges and nails; glass for windowpanes and bulbs; plastic for electric switches. Add the objects you see at home or in the classroom made from each material, and add a new row for a material that is missing, such as clay or rubber. Where does each material come from? Wood comes from trees, metals come from ore, glass is mostly made of sand, and cloth comes from plants like cotton or from animals like sheep.
Ask your grandparents whether things in their childhood were made of the same materials. Are there new materials now that they might not have seen, and are there materials they used that we do not use now? Why? Could you recognise a material with your eyes closed? Think about your spoon: is it smooth or rough, dull or shiny, and does it feel cold to the touch?
Take a metal spoon and five objects made of wood, metal, plastic, cloth and glass, and gently tap the spoon on each one. Listen to the sound each makes, and make your own words for the sounds, like ting-ting, dhum-dhum or dub-dub. Now compose your own beats, such as Ting, Ting, Thak, Thak, and Ting, Thak, Ting, Thak.
List five objects and pair each with a material that is not suitable, and explain why it will not work; for example, a paper umbrella tears in the rain. Khushi wrote that walls cannot be made of water, because a water wall would flow and fall down. We need solid things such as stones, bricks or wood to make walls, because solids do not change their shape.
Sort ink, a stone, smoke, ice, steam, a spoon, honey, a bottle, a bag and water into the tray for solids, the bottle for liquids and the balloon for gases. Add some objects of your own, and find at least three confusing ones, such as sand, a sponge or clay. Petroleum is a liquid found deep underground, and petrol, plastic, rubber and paraffin wax can be made from it; these leave waste that does not rot, and you will learn more about that in later classes.
List five natural things and five artificial things, and write the names of three materials we commonly see around us. Suppose you find a shining spoon and you do not know if it is metal or painted: you can tap it, feel if it is cold, scratch it gently and listen to its sound to find out. Match the pairs: transparent with the glass used in spectacles, translucent with a lamp shade made of paper, and opaque with a plate.

problem.en: Is a glass window transparent, translucent or opaque? Is wood?

text.en: We can see clearly through the glass window.
So glass is transparent.
We cannot see through wood, so wood is opaque.
A stone has its own shape: it is a solid.
Water flows and takes the shape of the cup: it is a liquid.
Air spreads out and is not seen: it is a gas.

why.en: It does not stay in a cup.

prompt.en: Explain how we can group things around us in two ways.

requiredIdeas.en: Say why you grouped them so

points.en: Things are made of materials such as wood, metal, glass and plastic.
We can see through transparent things, partly through translucent ones and not at all through opaque ones.
We choose materials for their properties.
Things can be solids, liquids or gases.
Natural things occur in nature, and artificial things are made by people.
We can test materials by looking, touching and tapping to find their properties.
Water walls cannot stand, because liquids flow, so we use solids for walls.
Petroleum gives us petrol, plastic and rubber, which are artificial materials.
